name: Citric acid

lead: Citric acid occurs in citrus fruit and is used everywhere from food to cleaning products. In skin care it mainly adjusts formula pH, and it is also listed among alpha hydroxy acids used in peels.
No controlled trials of citric acid alone as a lightening or resurfacing agent were found.

paras: As an AHA it is an acid that can exfoliate; as a buffer it sets product pH, and its citrate form binds metal ions.
Pure citric acid irritates skin and eyes at concentration, and repeated exposure can erode tooth enamel. It is GRAS in the US and E330 in the EU as a food additive.

label.generic: DEXTROSE MONOHYDRATE, SODIUM CITRATE, UNSPECIFIED FORM, AND CITRIC ACID MONOHYDRATE

lead: Citric acid is a weak organic acid found naturally in citrus fruits and an intermediate in the Krebs cycle.[1] It is widely used as a food acidulant (E330 in the EU) and, in cosmetics, as a pH adjuster; it is also classified as an alpha hydroxy acid and is an active ingredient in some chemical peels.[1][2]

Pure citric acid is a skin and eye irritant, and concentrated solutions can cause redness and pain.[1] The sources reviewed contain no completed controlled trials of citric acid as a stand-alone skin lightening or resurfacing agent.
infobox: pH adjuster, acidulant, AHA peel ingredient[1][2]
GRAS in the US; E330 in the EU[1][2]

paras: Citric acid is a triprotic acid with pKa values of about 3.1, 4.8 and 6.4, very soluble in water, and its citrate form binds metal ions, making it a chelating agent.[1] Industrial production is dominated by fermentation with the fungus Aspergillus niger, a method identified by James Currie in 1917.[1][2]
In creams, gels and liquids it serves as an acidulant to adjust pH.[1] As an AHA it is an active in chemical peels.[1]

Pure citric acid is a skin and eye irritant, and repeated exposure may erode tooth enamel.[1] It carries GHS "Warning" labelling for skin and eye irritation.[1] In its medical anticoagulant formulation, citrate toxicity can occur with infusion of citrate-containing blood products.[3]

No studies found of citric acid used alone as a skin lightening agent or peel. Registered trials involve other settings, such as a pilot trial of adjunctive acids in gingival melanin depigmentation (not yet recruiting) and dental implant and kidney stone studies.[4][5]

timeline.event: Scheele isolates citric acid from lemon juice.[1]
James Currie identifies Aspergillus niger fermentation.[1][2]
